name: David Torres

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for doing this, David. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent, with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions or any party, and everything you tell me is confidential. To start, what does a normal working day look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Right now I'm on a big distribution warehouse by the motorway junction, the size of six football pitches, for one of the large national contractors. I'm a carpenter by trade, so formwork for the concrete bases, temporary works, door frames for the office block on the front, but these days I'm also the one who runs the layout robot. It's a small machine that drives across the bare slab overnight and prints every wall and fixing point from the digital drawings, so in the morning the crews just follow the lines. I set it going at five in the evening, check its work at half six in the morning, then I'm on the tools the rest of the day.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy and what's hard?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I enjoy being the person who makes the new stuff work. The site manager comes to me now when the tablet drawings don't match, and I like that. The hard part is the older carpenters thinking I'm showing off, and the hours, because babysitting a robot overnight plus a full day on the tools is long, even if they pay me extra for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, fine, we keep the useful bits and get on with it. The layout robot would still be on site, the AI that helps me write the daily report would still be there, so nothing much would change. I wouldn't make a big deal of it online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be a little disappointed, because I've kind of bet my little corner of the job on this stuff. But only a little. I'm still a good carpenter, there's loads of work round here, and I'd still be the one who knows the gadgets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going as I am. Keep using the AI every day for the reports, the drawings and my kids' homework questions, which they love. Keep putting a bit each month into the index funds, the cheap ones that track the whole market.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Slightly let down, but calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you use AI for every day, concretely?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Morning, I photograph the slab and ask it to compare the robot's lines against the drawing, it flags anything odd. Afternoon, I talk into my phone in the van and it turns my rambling into a proper daily report. Evenings, Mateo asks it maths questions and I check it's not just giving him the answers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd bet your corner of the job on this. What did you mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I volunteered for the layout robot when nobody else wanted it, two years ago. It's made me useful in a new way, and I get paid a bit more for it. If AI stalls, that corner doesn't grow, but it doesn't vanish either.

S0.say: I'd say fine, we keep the useful bits and get on with it, since the layout robot and report-writing AI would still be there. I wouldn't make a big deal of it online.
S0.think: Privately he'd be slightly disappointed because he's built his niche around this technology. But he's still a good carpenter with plenty of local work, and still the one who knows the gadgets.
S0.do: Keeps using AI daily for reports, drawings and his kids' homework questions. Keeps putting money into low-cost index funds each month.
S0.quote: Afternoon, I talk into my phone in the van and it turns my rambling into a proper daily report.
S0.fieldNote: David is already living a version of the future on site, running a layout robot and using AI throughout his day. He describes his niche as a small bet that pays either way. The plateau mildly disappoints him but changes nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say get ahead of it, don't wait for it. Learn the tools, because the people who know them will be the ones still on site. I'd say help should be there for people who struggle, but complaining doesn't stop anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think this is good for me. I'm already the robot guy on this site, and a big contractor with lots of machines needs people who can run them and fix them. I'd expect to earn more, not less, though I'd feel for some of the older carpenters on the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the contractor to put me through their digital construction course straight away, and if they didn't, I'd pay for it, it's about fifteen hundred. I'd push for a second layout robot and another machine, maybe the drilling robot that does ceiling anchors. And I'd talk to my brother-in-law Rafa about his equipment rental firm adding robots to what they rent out, since I already have a small stake in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. Genuinely good, with a small pang for some of the guys.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who are you thinking of?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Stan, mostly. He's sixty, he's done formwork since before I was born, and he refuses to touch the tablet. He's brilliant with timber, better than me, but I can see a manager deciding he's too slow to change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you try to bring him along?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I've tried, honestly, and he tells me where to go, in a friendly way. I'd keep offering. But I'm not going to hold myself back to keep him company, that's not how it works.

S1.say: I'd say get ahead of it rather than wait, because those who know the tools will stay on site. Help should be there for people who struggle, but complaining doesn't stop anything.
S1.think: Privately he thinks this is good for him, as the site's robot person in a big contractor that will need machine operators. He expects to earn more, though he feels for older carpenters.
S1.do: Asks for the contractor's digital construction course and pays about fifteen hundred himself if refused, and pushes for more robots on site, like a ceiling-drilling machine. Talks to his brother-in-law about adding robots to the equipment rental firm he has a stake in.
S1.feel: Genuinely good, with a pang for older colleagues.
S1.quote: I'm not going to hold myself back to keep him company, that's not how it works.
S1.fieldNote: David sees steady disruption as an opportunity and moves first, both at work and with his money. His centrist mix shows: help for strugglers, but no patience for complaining. His honest line about not holding himself back for Stan was a little hard but clearly sincere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's happening, so let's be smart about it. Governments need to move fast with some support, but people need to move fast too. I'd say that at work and probably post about it, because I'm the one people ask.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it unsettles me, I won't lie. My whole plan is to be the person who runs the machines, and if the AI can run itself, that job doesn't last long either. But our money is partly in shares and partly in Rafa's rental business, and if robots are the future, that's where some of the money goes, so I'm not as exposed as I'd be on wages alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First month, I'd talk to Rafa about buying robots for the rental fleet, and I'd put in more of our savings, maybe twenty thousand, to make it happen. I'd keep my job running machines for the contractor as long as it lasts. We'd keep about a year of cash in the bank and leave the rest invested.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Busy and alert, but a bit off balance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said your money is in shares and the business. What happens if you're wrong about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then we've lost some, but not the house. Lucia's job as a dental hygienist is hands-on too, so I can't count on it forever, but it's steady for now. I'd rather own a bit of the robots than just hope someone keeps paying me to watch them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Mateo and Sofia?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That things are changing fast and it's exciting, and that Dad's going to be fine. Mateo would want to know if he can drive the robots, he's twelve. I'd let him come to the yard and see them, so it's not scary.

S2.say: I'd say it's happening, so be smart about it: governments need to move fast with support, and people need to move fast too. I'd say it at work and online, because I'm the one people ask.
S2.think: Privately it unsettles him because even running machines may not last if AI runs itself. But his money is partly in shares and his brother-in-law's rental firm, so he's less exposed than he would be on wages alone.
S2.do: Puts about twenty thousand of savings into buying robots for the rental fleet in the first month and keeps running machines for the contractor while that lasts. Holds about a year of cash and leaves the rest invested.
S2.feel: Uneasy: busy and alert but a bit off balance.
S2.quote: I'd rather own a bit of the robots than just hope someone keeps paying me to watch them.
S2.fieldNote: David hedges with assets, not just skills, which keeps him steadier than most in the fast picture. He admits his operator plan has a short shelf life under full AGI. His instinct to show his son the robots so they aren't scary was a nice detail.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a gift, use it. Learn, save, invest, change if you need to. I'd say it to the younger guys especially.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is enough for me to get set up properly. I'd move over to Rafa's business full-time, managing the robot fleet, setting them up on sites, training crews. By the time AGI is fully here, I'd be on the owning side of it rather than the working side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, I'd do the digital construction course and a robot maintenance certificate. Year two, I'd go part-time at the contractor and part-time at Rafa's. By year three, I'd be full-time at the rental firm, with a bigger stake, and we'd have kept up the index fund payments the whole time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like I've got a plan and it's a good one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Lucia say about you leaving a secure job for your brother-in-law's business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd say, you and Rafa better not fall out. She's right, family and money is risky. We'd get a proper agreement on paper first, with a lawyer, even though Rafa would be offended.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that could go wrong with that plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Plenty. The big rental companies could squeeze us out, or the robots could get cheap enough that contractors just buy their own. I don't know, nobody does. But I'd rather take a swing than stand still.

S3.say: I'd say five years is a gift, so use it to learn, save, invest and change if needed. I'd say it to the younger workers especially.
S3.think: Privately he thinks five years is enough to move to his brother-in-law's rental firm full-time, managing a robot fleet. He'd aim to be on the owning side rather than the working side when AGI arrives.
S3.do: Takes a digital construction course and a robot maintenance certificate in year one, splits his time between the contractor and the rental firm in year two, and goes full-time there with a bigger stake by year three. Keeps up index fund payments throughout and gets a written agreement with a lawyer.
S3.feel: Calm, with a plan he believes in.
S3.quote: She'd say, you and Rafa better not fall out.
S3.fieldNote: With five years David has a detailed, staged plan to move from wages to ownership. He weighs the family-business risk and plans to put it on paper. His uncertainty is honest, but his appetite for risk carries him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough for anyone to get ready if they start now. Governments should help with retraining, but people should take charge themselves. Nothing dramatic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years is easy for me. I'd be fifty-three, the mortgage mostly paid, investments grown, and probably running the robot side at Rafa's. My worry would be more about other people than about us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't rush. I'd keep my job, keep growing the stake in Rafa's business, keep the index funds going. Somewhere around year four or five I'd make the move to the rental firm full-time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about, then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Stan, still, if he's working at seventy, which he says he will be. And the apprentices, because where do they learn if the robots do the simple jobs? I'd like the rental business to take on a couple of apprentices to learn the machines, that'd be something useful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said people should take charge themselves. What about people who can't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then they need help, real help, and I'd pay my taxes for it. I'm not saying everyone's like me. I'm just saying, if you can move, move.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is enough for anyone to get ready if they start now. Governments should help with retraining, but people should take charge themselves.
S4.think: Privately ten years is easy for him, with the mortgage mostly paid, investments grown and probably a role running robots at his brother-in-law's firm. His worries are about other people more than his family.
S4.do: Keeps his job while growing his stake in the rental business and continuing index fund payments. Moves to the rental firm full-time around year four or five and hopes to take on apprentices to learn the machines.
S4.quote: I'm not saying everyone's like me. I'm just saying, if you can move, move.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, David relaxes completely and his attention turns outward to older workers and apprentices. When pressed, he backed real support for people who can't adapt and said he'd pay taxes for it. His centrism shows in that mix of self-reliance and fairness.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Not because I'd sink, I think we'd be fine, but because there'd be chaos, and chaos is bad for business and bad for people like Stan. What would help is a government plan ready on the shelf: retraining money, a safety net for older workers, and clear rules for firms bringing in robots so it's not a free-for-all.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who's already working with robots, like me. There are people on sites right now who know what these machines can and can't do. Ask us, not just the people selling them.

headlineQuote: Ask us, not just the people selling them.
portrait: David is a 43-year-old carpenter on a huge warehouse build who has become the site's robot operator, using AI every day for drawings, reports and his kids' homework. He has index funds and a stake in his brother-in-law's equipment rental business, so his family's security doesn't rest on wages alone. He stays calm through the plateau and steady pictures, is unsettled but busy when AGI comes in two years, and with five or ten years plans to move into managing a robot rental fleet. He believes in moving first, but backs real help for those who can't.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because of the chaos it would cause, especially for older workers like his colleague Stan.
whatWouldHelp: A government plan ready in advance, with retraining money, a safety net for older workers and clear rules for firms bringing in robots.
